From Wiktionary, the free dictionary
See also: cassé and câsse

English

[edit]

Etymology

[edit]

From French casse (literally “breakage”), from casser (“to break”).[1]

Noun

[edit]

casse (uncountable)

  1. A fault in wine, caused by an enzyme, making it turn from red to brown, or white to yellow, on exposure to air.

See also

[edit]
  • casse-croute

References

[edit]
  1. ^ “casse”, in Merriam-Webster Online Dictionary, Springfield, Mass.: Merriam-Webster, 1996–present.

Anagrams

[edit]
  • cases, SCEAs, SECAs

French

[edit]

Etymology 1

[edit]

From casser.

Pronunciation

[edit]
  • IPA(key): /kas/ ~ /kɑs/ (/ɑ/ in dialects with this phoneme)
  • Audio (Paris):(file)
  • Rhymes: -ɑs

Verb

[edit]

casse

  1. inflection of casser:
    1. first/third-person singular present indicative/subjunctive
    2. second-person singular imperative
Derived terms
[edit]
  • casse-noisette
  • casse-noix
  • casse-pieds
  • casse-tête

Noun

[edit]

casse m (plural casses)

  1. (slang) burglary, break-in
Derived terms
[edit]
  • chien de la casse

Noun

[edit]

casse f (plural casses)

  1. breakage (act of breaking)
    Antonym: non-casse
  2. (colloquial, figuratively) ruckus; mayhem
    Synonym: grabuge
    Il va y avoir de la casse ! ― (please add an English translation of this usage example)
  3. breaker's yard, wreck yard
Derived terms
[edit]
  • non-casse

Etymology 2

[edit]

Borrowed from Italian cassa, from Latin capsa. Doublet of châsse and caisse.

Noun

[edit]

casse f (plural casses)

  2. (typography, informatics) case
    sensible à la casse ― case-sensitive

Further reading

[edit]
  • “casse”, in Dictionnaire français en ligne Larousse
  • Littré, Émile (1873–1878), “casse”, in Dictionnaire de la langue française, Paris: L. Hachette
  • “casse” in Dictionnaire Le Robert.
  • “casse”, in Trésor de la langue française informatisé [Digitized Treasury of the French Language], 2012

Anagrams

[edit]
  • cases, cessa

Latin

[edit]

Adjective

[edit]

casse

  1. vocative masculine singular of cassus

References

[edit]
  • “casse”, in Charlton T. Lewis and Charles Short (1879), A Latin Dictionary, Oxford: Clarendon Press
  • "casse", in Charles du Fresne du Cange, Glossarium Mediæ et Infimæ Latinitatis (augmented edition with additions by D. P. Carpenterius, Adelungius and others, edited by Léopold Favre, 1883–1887)

Occitan

[edit]

Etymology

[edit]

From Old Occitan [Term?], from Vulgar Latin *cassanus (attested in Medieval Latin as casnus), probably from Gaulish kassanos. Compare French chêne (Old French chesne, chasne), Franco-Provençal châno. See also Aragonese caixico, Spanish quejigo.

Pronunciation

[edit]
  • IPA(key): [ˈkase]
  • Audio (Béarn):(file)

Noun

[edit]

casse m (plural casses)

  1. oak

Derived terms

[edit]
  • cassanha
  • cassenada
  • cassenat
  • cassenòla

Dialectal variants

[edit]
  • casso (Gascony)
  • chassanh (Limousin)

Synonyms

[edit]
  • garric
  • roire

Old French

[edit]

Alternative forms

[edit]
  • case, quase

Etymology

[edit]

    Inherited from Latin capsa.

    Pronunciation

    [edit]
    • IPA(key): /ˈkasə/

    Noun

    [edit]

    casse oblique singular, f (oblique plural casses, nominative singular casse, nominative plural casses)

    1. Old Northern French form of chasse

    Descendants

    [edit]
    • Norman: câsse
    • → Middle English: case, caas, casse
      • English: case
      • Yola: kaase
      • → Irish: cás

    References

    [edit]
    • casse on the Anglo-Norman On-Line Hub
    • Frédéric Godefroy (1880–1902), “caisse”, in Dictionnaire de l’ancienne langue française et de tous ses dialectes du IXe au XVe siècle […], Paris: F[riedrich] Vieweg; Émile Bouillon, →OCLC.

    Portuguese

    [edit]

    Verb

    [edit]

    casse

    1. inflection of cassar:
      1. first/third-person singular present subjunctive
      2. third-person singular imperative
